blocks.text: A 69-year-old right-handed woman is mid-sentence when her speech stops. Her right face and right hand sag and she cannot find words, yet she can still lift her right leg off the bed. The pattern of what is lost and what is spared is a map of one artery's territory.

blocks.markdown: The brain receives about 15% of cardiac output and has almost no energy reserve, so interruption of flow causes neuronal injury within minutes. Blood arrives by two systems. The paired **internal carotid arteries (ICA)** form the **anterior circulation**. The paired **vertebral arteries** join at the pontomedullary junction to form the **basilar artery**, the **posterior circulation**. The basilar artery ends by dividing into the two **posterior cerebral arteries (PCA)**. **Stroke** is sudden focal neurological deficit due to vascular cause, most commonly **ischaemic** (arterial occlusion by thrombus or embolus) and less often haemorrhagic.

**The three cerebral arteries.**

- **Anterior cerebral artery (ACA)**: a terminal branch of the ICA that runs in the longitudinal fissure above the corpus callosum. It supplies the **medial surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes**, including the **paracentral lobule** (leg areas of the motor and sensory cortex), plus the anterior corpus callosum and part of the basal ganglia.
- **Middle cerebral artery (MCA)**: the larger terminal branch of the ICA, running in the lateral sulcus. It supplies most of the **lateral surface** of the hemisphere: the motor and sensory cortex for the **face and arm**, the **Broca and Wernicke areas** in the dominant hemisphere, parts of the parietal and temporal lobes, and (by deep **lenticulostriate branches**) the **internal capsule and basal ganglia**.
- **Posterior cerebral artery (PCA)**: from the basilar artery; supplies the **occipital lobe (primary visual cortex)**, the inferomedial temporal lobe and the thalamus (via perforators).

rows: Medial frontal and parietal lobes (leg areas)
Contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss (greater than arm); apathy or abulia
Lateral hemisphere: face and arm areas, language areas
Contralateral face and arm weakness and sensory loss, visual field defect; aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant)
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia (macular sparing is common)
blocks.caption: The homunculus explains the pattern: the leg lies on the medial surface (ACA), the face and arm on the lateral surface (MCA).

blocks.title: Why an ACA occlusion spares the arm and face
blocks.prompt: A patient has weakness of the left leg and foot, much milder in the left arm, and a normal face. Which artery is occluded, and which side?

steps.text: On the motor homunculus the leg area is on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule, whereas the arm and face areas lie on the lateral convexity.
The medial surface is supplied by the ACA; the lateral convexity by the MCA.
Left-sided weakness means the right motor cortex is affected, because the corticospinal tract crosses below.

blocks.answer: Right ACA occlusion: the contralateral (left) leg is weak, with relative sparing of the arm and face.

blocks.title: Circle of Willis
blocks.text: The circle of Willis is an anastomotic ring of arteries at the base of the brain that links the anterior and posterior circulations and the right and left sides. It is formed by the anterior communicating artery, the two anterior cerebral arteries (A1 segments), the two internal carotid arteries, the two posterior communicating arteries and the two posterior cerebral arteries (P1 segments, from the basilar artery).

blocks.markdown: **Role.** The circle provides **collateral circulation**: if one artery is narrowed or occluded, flow can be redistributed. For example, with a slowly developing ICA stenosis, blood can reach the ipsilateral ACA and MCA through the anterior communicating artery from the opposite ICA, or through the posterior communicating artery from the basilar system. In practice the circle is **complete in only a minority of people**, so its protective effect varies. Its junctions are also the commonest sites of **berry aneurysms**, which cause subarachnoid haemorrhage when they rupture.

blocks.title: Collateral flow after a carotid occlusion
blocks.prompt: A left ICA is gradually occluded, but the patient has no symptoms. Explain how the left hemisphere stays perfused.

steps.text: The right ICA continues to supply the right ACA, and the anterior communicating artery connects the right and left ACAs.
Blood flows from the right ACA across the anterior communicating artery into the left ACA, which fills the left MCA retrogradely through the left ICA terminus.
Blood may also pass from the basilar artery through the left posterior communicating artery to the left ICA terminus.

blocks.answer: The circle of Willis redistributes flow through the anterior and posterior communicating arteries, so the left hemisphere is perfused despite ICA occlusion.

blocks.markdown: **Middle cerebral artery infarct.** Occlusion of the main MCA trunk produces: contralateral **hemiparesis of the face and arm** (greater than the leg); contralateral **hemisensory loss** of the same distribution; **contralateral homonymous hemianopia** from involvement of the optic radiation; **gaze preference toward the lesion**; and cortical signs that depend on the hemisphere. In the **dominant** (usually left) hemisphere: **aphasia** (expressive, receptive or global). In the **non-dominant** (usually right) hemisphere: **hemispatial neglect** of the left side and **anosognosia**. Occlusion of the deep **lenticulostriate** branches causes small infarcts in the internal capsule or basal ganglia (lacunar infarcts), commonly giving a **pure motor hemiparesis** of face, arm and leg together, because corticospinal fibres are densely packed in the internal capsule.

blocks.title: Face and arm versus leg
blocks.text: Face and arm worse than leg suggests MCA cortical territory. Leg worse than arm suggests ACA. A visual field defect with no weakness suggests PCA. Equal weakness of face, arm and leg with no cortical signs suggests a deep lacunar lesion in the internal capsule.

points: The ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, the MCA the lateral hemisphere, and the PCA the occipital lobe and inferomedial temporal lobe.
The circle of Willis links the anterior and posterior circulations through the anterior and posterior communicating arteries and provides collateral flow, though it is often incomplete.
MCA infarct causes contralateral face and arm weakness and sensory loss, hemianopia, and aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant); lenticulostriate occlusion causes lacunar pure motor stroke.

questions.stem: Which artery supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes?

distractorRationale.a: The MCA supplies the lateral surface.
distractorRationale.c: The PCA supplies the occipital lobe and inferomedial temporal lobe.
distractorRationale.d: The basilar artery supplies the brainstem and gives rise to the PCAs.

questions.explanation: The ACA runs along the medial surface of the hemisphere and supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, including the paracentral lobule.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man suddenly cannot see to his left in either eye. Examination shows a left homonymous hemianopia with no weakness or sensory loss. Which artery is most likely occluded?

distractorRationale.b: An MCA stem occlusion would also cause weakness and sensory loss.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the right occipital cortex represents the left visual field and is supplied by the right PCA.
distractorRationale.d: A left PCA infarct would cause a right homonymous hemianopia.

questions.explanation: The right visual cortex receives the left visual field from both eyes, and the right PCA supplies the right occipital lobe. An isolated left homonymous hemianopia without motor or sensory loss therefore localises to the right PCA territory.

questions.stem: Which deficit is characteristic of an anterior cerebral artery infarct?

options.text: Contralateral leg weakness greater than arm weakness
Contralateral face and arm weakness greater than leg weakness

questions.correctOptionText: Contralateral leg weakness greater than arm weakness

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the leg area of the motor cortex is on the medial surface.
distractorRationale.c: Hemianopia indicates the PCA or optic pathway.

questions.explanation: The ACA supplies the paracentral lobule, which contains the leg representation. Its occlusion causes contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss.

questions.stem: Which arteries directly connect the internal carotid circulation with the posterior cerebral arteries in the circle of Willis?

distractorRationale.a: The anterior communicating artery links the two ACAs.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: each posterior communicating artery joins the ICA to the PCA.
distractorRationale.c: The vertebral arteries form the basilar artery.
distractorRationale.d: The MCA is a terminal branch of the ICA, outside the circle.

questions.explanation: The posterior communicating artery runs from the internal carotid to the posterior cerebral artery and links the anterior and posterior circulations.

questions.stem: Which statement about the anterior communicating artery is correct?

options.text: It connects the two anterior cerebral arteries across the midline
It connects the basilar artery to the internal carotid artery
It joins the middle cerebral arteries
It is a branch of the vertebral artery

questions.correctOptionText: It connects the two anterior cerebral arteries across the midline

distractorRationale.b: That is the posterior communicating artery.
distractorRationale.c: The MCAs are not joined by a communicating artery.
distractorRationale.d: It is not a branch of the vertebral artery.

questions.explanation: The anterior communicating artery completes the front of the circle by linking the two ACAs. It allows flow to cross between hemispheres.

questions.stem: True or false: the circle of Willis can provide collateral flow to a hemisphere when one internal carotid artery is narrowed.
questions.explanation: The communicating arteries allow blood to be redistributed between sides and between the anterior and posterior circulations. The protection is only partial because the circle is complete in only a minority of people.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old right-handed man with atrial fibrillation has a right middle cerebral artery occlusion. Which combination is most likely?

options.text: Right face and arm weakness with expressive aphasia
Left face and arm weakness, left sensory loss and left hemispatial neglect
Left leg weakness and urinary incontinence

questions.correctOptionText: Left face and arm weakness, left sensory loss and left hemispatial neglect

distractorRationale.a: Right-sided weakness with aphasia indicates a left (dominant) MCA lesion.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a right MCA lesion causes left-sided deficits, with neglect from the non-dominant parietal lobe.
distractorRationale.d: Right hemianopia would indicate left-sided visual pathway damage.

questions.explanation: The right MCA supplies the right lateral hemisphere, controlling the left face and arm. In a right-handed person the right hemisphere is non-dominant, so parietal damage produces neglect rather than aphasia.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden weakness of the left face, arm and leg to an equal degree, with normal sensation, language and visual fields. A small infarct is found in the right internal capsule. Which vessels are most likely involved?

options.text: Lenticulostriate branches of the right middle cerebral artery
Cortical branches of the right anterior cerebral artery

questions.correctOptionText: Lenticulostriate branches of the right middle cerebral artery

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these deep penetrating branches supply the internal capsule.
distractorRationale.b: ACA cortical branches would produce leg-predominant weakness.
distractorRationale.c: A left PCA lesion would not cause left weakness.
distractorRationale.d: Basilar occlusion causes brainstem and bilateral signs.

questions.explanation: The corticospinal fibres are tightly packed in the internal capsule, so a small lacunar infarct from occlusion of lenticulostriate branches produces equal weakness of the contralateral face, arm and leg without cortical signs. These deep branches arise from the MCA.

questions.stem: Explain, using the arterial territories and the motor homunculus, why a large occlusion of the middle cerebral artery weakens the contralateral face and arm more than the leg.
markingGuide: The MCA supplies the lateral convexity of the hemisphere
The face and hand areas of the primary motor cortex lie on the lateral convexity
The leg area lies on the medial surface in the paracentral lobule, supplied by the ACA
The leg is therefore relatively spared
Weakness is contralateral because the corticospinal tracts cross at the pyramids
May add sensory loss, hemianopia, aphasia or neglect
questions.explanation: The motor homunculus runs over the convexity to the medial surface, so the face and arm areas fall in the MCA territory and the leg in the ACA territory. An MCA occlusion therefore weakens the contralateral face and arm most.

questions.stem: Name the arteries that form the circle of Willis and explain two ways in which the circle protects the brain and one clinical reason it is important.
markingGuide: Anterior communicating, anterior cerebral (A1), internal carotid, posterior communicating and posterior cerebral (P1) arteries
Connects the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems
Connects the left and right sides
Provides collateral flow if one vessel is occluded or stenosed
Circle is often incomplete, so protection varies
Aneurysms commonly arise at junctions of the circle and cause subarachnoid haemorrhage
questions.explanation: The circle is a ring that links the carotid and basilar territories across the midline, allowing redistribution of flow. Its branching points are also the usual sites of berry aneurysms.
